theory: A program can pass a task's three asserts by coincidence (SeedLM-36, 37). Coders trained apart rarely make the same coincidental program their first choice, so a behaviour that many of them propose independently is more likely to be the task's real one. Single-coder overrides of the engine gained under the lenient judge and nothing under the strict one (pyx_fill, pyx_override); the committee's choice is the test of whether agreement survives
rule: the engine's program where the engine is confident (70 of the development tasks); elsewhere the first verified program (SeedLM-15's cache) that most of SeedLM-32's 24 cached coders agree with on the 24 probes (rulecoder.consensus.compare, ties to the earlier coder in the fixed list, SeedLM-10's vote); the engine's program where no coder proposes one
baseline_same_machinery: the same rule with s5-var's cached program in place of the vote (the main system without its tie-breaking)
primary_measure: development fifth, judged strictly (asserts, then no conflict with the reference solution on the probes) and leniently (asserts): supported if strict above 58 (the main system, reports/seedlm/holdout4_s5-var_strict.json) and lenient at least 69; not supported if strict at most 58

outcome.primary: development fifth: the committee rule 64 lenient, 55 strict; strict at most 58: not supported (reports/seedlm/consensus38_development.json)
secondary: the same rule with s5-var's program: 67 lenient, 56 strict; the engine alone: 65 and 56
outcome.reading: On the 24 tasks where the engine is unsure or silent, the program most cached coders propose is no more often truly right than s5-var's own; the coders' first choices there are mostly the same coincidences, so their agreement is not independent evidence
